extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric / aspiring orators
extracted.subtask_description: A checklist of rhetorical and forensic qualities used to judge or cultivate excellence in classical public speaking (voice, language, invention, action, learning, method, emotional force, etc.). Drawn from examples and anti‑patterns in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity and correctness of language
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure and correct style is the groundwork, the very basis and foundation, upon which an Orator must build his other accomplishments; an accurate choice of words is the foundation of Eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly praises speakers (Caesar, Laelius, Scipio) who speak with linguistic purity and contrasts them with corrupt or provincial usages. Reforming language to a standard (avoiding domestic barbarisms) is recommended. Purity applies both to common speech and to written works (e.g., concise, correct historical prose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom and fluency of elocution
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of elocution and tolerable fluency of expression are important to be reckoned an orator; fluent, voluble flow of expression supports reputation as an ornamented speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Curio gained reputation from a 'tolerable freedom of Elocution'; others praised for easy, voluble flow. Fluent elocution helps in both private and public causes; lack of fluency undermines otherwise good matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of voice (sonorous, sweet, manly)
rubrics_metrics.description: The voice — its strength, sweetness, sonority and manliness — is a central attribute of an effective speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good voice can disguise other defects (Catulus, P. Lentulus). Poor or harsh pronunciation (Cotta's rustic utterance) or excessive rapidity can reduce clarity (Visellius Varro). A 'sonorous and manly' voice enhances dignity and persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action and gesture (delivery / physical presence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Action—gesture, sudden breaks, exclamations, warmth and liveliness of movement—and the dignity of deportment materially affect an orator's perceived merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action can conceal defects (Cn. Lentulus, P. Lentulus); graceful gesture and presence add credit (P. Lentulus). Yet action without substance or overacting (violent hurry) is criticized (Cosconius). Balance and naturalness preferred over affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to move the passions (emotional force)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to 'move and alarm the passions' is described as of much greater efficacy than merely instructing or pleasing; it is a chief merit of an orator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers who are incapable of exciting emotion (Calidius in the poisoning prosecution) are judged deficient even if polished. Emotional force must be genuine; absence of visible emotion can weaken persuasive impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness / richness of ideas (invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive power and richness in producing ideas and arguments are essential; 'poverty of invention' is seen as a major deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some rely on other qualities to conceal lack of invention (action, presence). Systems like Hermagoras are cited as aids to invention; methodical preparation and digestion of subject matter compensate for weaker natural invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning and erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: Erudition, knowledge of literature (especially Greek learning), and thorough study are sources of rhetorical talent for some speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M. Piso's talents derived from Grecian literature; learning supplies material and subtlety of thought. Excessive learning without application or feeling can produce coldness; learning should be put into practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and precision in reasoning and idea-digestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy in inventing and digesting ideas — precise, careful handling of argument — is highly valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. Macer is praised for extraordinary accuracy in inventing and digesting ideas, though shown off as a quibbler; precision must be paired with persuasive style to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity of presence and deportment
rubrics_metrics.description: A dignified presence and genteel deportment (correct and graceful gesture, noble bearing) contribute substantially to an orator's merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some speakers (P. Lentulus, Cn. Pompeius) derive much credit from presence alone; presence supports reception of arguments and can elevate otherwise middling abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry, application and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefatigable application, industry, and frequent practice in public speaking or exercises lead to marked improvement and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: L. Turius, Q. Pompeius and others show that steady practice and diligence can overcome indifferent genius. Regular composition and declamation (daily essays) are recommended (as in Caesar's case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method and organization (digestion / arrangement of subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodical preparation, organizing and digesting the subject before speaking — following a system (e.g., Hermagoras) — is crucial for clear invention and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hermagoras' system supplies fixed rules to expedite invention and methodize subjects. Always digesting the subject prevents mistakes and helps in public pleading; method substitutes for pure natural gift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and clarity (especially in prose/history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concise, correct, and elegant brevity of expression (particularly in historical writing) is highly pleasing and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caesar's commentaries praised as plain, correct and graceful, 'in a kind of undress.' In history, brevity is preferred to ornament; clarity should trump excessive embellishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figures/ornaments/metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate use of rhetorical figures, metaphor and ornamentation enliven and embellish style when well-managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calidius is master of 'figures'—metaphors that fit their place and do not usurp others'. Ornament should be numerous yet not ostentatious; overuse or misplaced metaphors are to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to audience and occasion (popular vs. learned style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in tailoring speech to the audience — addressing 'the many' in a popular manner or adopting learned refinement for polished audiences — affects success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Q. Arrius rose by devoting himself to popular occasions; some speakers are better in political debates than in judicial trials. The orator must recognize forum-specific expectations and adapt style accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affectation and artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalness — speaking without the appearance of artifice or affectation — is preferable and signals genuine mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caesar is commended for splendour 'without the least appearance of artifice or affectation.' Affected manner weakens credibility even if technically correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tempo and audibility (avoid excessive rapidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery tempo must preserve clarity; excessive rapidity of style or speech causes obscurity and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visellius Varro's 'excessively quick and rapid' style rendered his language obscure despite good choice of words. Controlled pace aids comprehension and persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament and moderation (avoid immoderate vehemence or coldness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperament must suit the art: immoderate vehemence appears as madness, while excessive coldness or indifference deprives speech of persuasive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fimbria's immoderate vehemence made him seem mad; others are faulted for being too cold (C. Censorinus). Balance emotional energy to the subject and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of style to subject (judicial vs. political)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different subjects and forums demand different rhetorical emphases (e.g., more passion in judicial trials; different tone in political debate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: L. Lentulus was too warm for judicial advocacy but adequate in political debate. The orator should select tone, force and ornament appropriate to the matter at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use delivery to mask lack of substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying solely on action, voice or presence to conceal poverty of invention or expression is an anti-pattern and can be exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several examples (Cn. Lentulus, P. Lentulus) show action/presence hiding other defects; such masking may work with audiences but is not a substitute for solid argument and invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nicety of diction and careful arrangement of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact placement of words, nicety of phrasing and harmonious structuring of periods produce a refined, mosaic-like style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calidius' language is likened to 'a curious piece of Mosaic-work' — every word exactly where it should be. Such precision enhances clarity and aesthetic effect but must not replace force.
